claims.text: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is the alloy system under study.
The baseline alloy is vacuum-sintered at 1400 °C for 18 h.
Slow cooling after sintering produces a multiphase microstructure.
The slow-cooled microstructure consists specifically of β-BCC1, β-BCC2, and α-HCP phases.
The baseline alloy contains about 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed intervention is rapid water quenching after sintering under a controlled oxygen atmosphere targeting approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Rapid quenching suppresses formation of the α-HCP phase.
Suppressing α-HCP by rapid quenching retains a metastable single-phase β-BCC microstructure.
Controlled processing will distribute interstitial oxygen homogeneously in the β-BCC matrix.
Interstitial oxygen provides solid-solution strengthening in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Eliminating secondary phases reduces weak interfaces.
Reducing weak interfaces preserves thermal and irradiation stability.
Quenching with controlled oxygen will significantly increase high-temperature yield strength relative to the slow-cooled multiphase baseline.
The treated alloy will retain oxidation resistance comparable to that of the slow-cooled baseline.
The treated alloy will retain irradiation tolerance comparable to that of the slow-cooled baseline.
The proposed mechanical benefit should hold from approximately 750 °C to 1100 °C.
Excessive or otherwise deviating oxygen content may produce brittle phases.
Deviations in oxygen content or cooling rate may cause a loss of irradiation stability.
The cited study performed compression testing on this alloy at 800–1100 °C and a strain rate of 10^-4 s^-1.
Failure to improve yield strength significantly, or degradation of oxidation or irradiation stability, is designated as a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes a controlled increase in oxygen, but both the initial state and intervention target are approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, so no quantified increase relative to the baseline is actually specified.
